title: Splitting the Archive
setting: a records office split across buildings

post.author: u/glasshouse_nights_tabitha
post.title: I'm the night clerk in the newest of our county's record buildings. A birth registered on Monday was in none of them until Thursday, and I could see his box from my desk.

blocks.text: I file records at night for the Kelderby County Records Office. The archive outgrew one building long ago, so it's split by year: the Maltings holds 1850 to 1939, the Drill Hall 1940 to 1999, and the Glasshouse, mine, 2000 onward. Every record has a number, given in the order it was filed: 1,200,000 of them. A card at the front desk, the directory, says which building holds which years, and every lookup goes through it.

Every new registration is dated this year, so every one comes to me. 1,200 arrive each night, and I can file 600. At dawn the other 600 wait by the door for the day shift. Across the lane the Maltings and the Drill Hall stand dark all night.

So on Monday 2 November the county opened a fourth building, the Ropewalk, and moved the boundary. At noon Mr Lowther, the county archivist, changed the directory: 2013 onward, the Ropewalk. The 120,000 records from 2013 on went across in vans, 30,000 a day, oldest boxes first, landing at 17:00, Monday to Thursday. From Monday night every new record went to the Ropewalk.
On Tuesday morning a mother came in for a copy of her son's birth certificate. He was registered on Monday at 09:12: No. 1,200,000, the last record filed in my building before noon.

Tue 3 Nov 10:41  lookup No. 1,200,000   birth, registered Mon 2 Nov 09:12
                 directory              2013 onward: the Ropewalk
                 the Ropewalk           NOT FOUND
                 the Glasshouse         not our years
                 Maltings, Drill Hall   not our years
Wed 4 Nov 09:30  lookup No. 1,200,000   NOT FOUND in any building
Thu 5 Nov 17:00  van 4 of 4 shelved at the Ropewalk: 30,000 records
Thu 5 Nov 17:06  lookup No. 1,200,000   the Ropewalk: FOUND
Every building said it had never held him. On Tuesday night I could see his box on my shelf.

Nothing was lost. It just wasn't anywhere. Now the Ropewalk's night clerk leaves 600 at the door each dawn, and my nights are quiet. The county says it will need a fifth building within two years. Mr Lowther says the vans were too slow. What should he change before then?

blocks.label: directory_tuesday_1041.png

diagram.aria: Tabitha's drawing of Tuesday 3 November at 10:41. The front desk looks up record No. 1,200,000 and gets NOT FOUND. The directory, switched at noon on Monday, says 2013 onward: the Ropewalk. The Maltings holds 1850 to 1939 and the Drill Hall 1940 to 1999, both dark at night. The Ropewalk holds 2013 onward but has only 30,000 records so far, from van 1 of 4. The Glasshouse now holds 2000 to 2012 by the directory, but 90,000 records from 2013 on still sit on its shelves waiting for vans.

notes.text: Tuesday 10:41: 90,000 records from 2013 on sit in no building the directory names

blocks.caption: My drawing of Tuesday at 10:41. Since noon on Monday the directory has sent every record from 2013 on to the Ropewalk, but only Monday's van had landed: 30,000 records. The other 90,000 were still on the Glasshouse's shelves, and the Glasshouse turns away any year the directory doesn't give it. The Maltings and the Drill Hall hold their years and sit dark at night.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Three things to look at before anyone picks a fix. One: every split has a shard key, the one value that decides which building a record lives in. Yours is the year. Which year does every new record carry, so which building takes all of them, and what are the others doing at 03:00? Two: the directory. On Tuesday at 10:41, which building did it name for No. 1,200,000, and where was the box? Count how many records were in that state on Monday afternoon. Three: there will be a fifth building. For any rule you consider, ask how many of the 1,200,000 would ride in vans that week, how many would answer not found while they ride, and how many buildings someone asking for every record from 1931 would have to ask.

replies.author: u/glasshouse_nights_tabitha
replies.text: At noon on Monday, 120,000: everything from 2013 on. 90,000 on Tuesday morning. And something I forgot: in the spring the Ellingham family's solicitors bring in their deposit, 2,400 papers from 1931, all filed under one deposit number.

comments.author: u/shelfmark_hartwell
comments.text: Forty years in county archives. Ranges by year are how archives have always worked, and for good reason: a researcher asks for 1931, and 1931 sits on one run of shelves in one building. Scatter a year across four buildings and every question becomes four errands. Your county's only mistake was moving 2013 to 2026 at all, with the card already pointing at the Ropewalk. Next time, move nothing. Open the new building empty on New Year's Day for the new year. Every year stays where it was filed, the directory only ever gains a line, and no box ever rides in a van.

comments.author: u/remainder_mirela
comments.text: Or drop the card. At my last job our customer rows lived on database number hash(customer id) mod 3, where a hash turns a value into a number, the same number every time. Anyone can work out where a row lives on a scrap of paper, so there's no list to keep, and new rows spread evenly whatever year they carry.

comments.author: u/one_roof_fenella
comments.text: Honest answer from a parish office: we had the same mess across three halls, and in 2019 we moved everything into one old mill with room for twice what we had. One roof, one card, no boundaries, two clerks at night. It's still fine. It won't be fine forever, but it bought us years.

reply.prompt: Kelderby will need a fifth building within two years, and more after that. What should Mr Lowther change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Hash record numbers into 120 fixed partitions; when a building opens, move whole ones, updating the directory as each lands.
options.part2: Mr Lowther rebuilt the archive over the winter as 120 fixed partitions. A record's partition is a hash of its number, each building holds 30, and the directory lists all 120. The switch itself was one big move: 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records changed building, because every record's place was decided again. He moved them a partition at a time, copying first, then changing that partition's line in the directory, then clearing the old shelves, and no lookup failed. Each partition keeps its own index by date. Now each building files 300 a night and nobody waits at dawn. In March the Tannery opened: 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, 8 vans, and nothing was unreachable for a minute. The price came in two places. A question for every record from 1931 now goes to all five buildings, every partition reading its by-date index, and the answer comes when the slowest building replies. And in April the Ellingham deposit arrived, 2,400 papers under one deposit number: one partition, so the Tannery got 2,640 records that night. Deposits are now keyed by deposit and item number.
options.senior: Sharding splits both storage and writes, and the shard key decides everything after. Years keep a range in one place but send every new record to one building. A hash of the record number spreads the writes, at the price of asking every building for a range, so keep a by-date index in each partition. Many more fixed partitions than buildings make opening one a matter of moving whole partitions, a quarter of the records for a fourth building, and a directory switched one partition at a time keeps every record findable during the move. One hot key still needs splitting.

options.text: Keep filing by year, but open each new building empty on New Year's Day for that year's records, so no box ever has to move again.
options.verdict: Moves nothing, still one hot building
options.part2: On 1 January the Tannery opened, empty, for 2027. Nothing moved, nothing went missing, and the directory gained one line. Then, on the first night of 2027, every new record went to the Tannery. Its night clerk files 600 of the 1,200, and 600 wait at dawn, while four buildings across the lane stand dark: busiest building 1,200 a night, average 240. In April the Ellingham deposit, 2,400 papers dated 1931, all went to the Maltings, which filed 600 and left 1,800 for the morning. The county is already asking what happens in 2028.
options.senior: Ranges by year keep each year in one place, and an empty building for a new year moves nothing. But dates only grow, so every new record still lands on one building: the hot partition just moves on 1 January. MongoDB's docs say it plainly: with an always-increasing shard key every insert goes to one chunk, and its shard becomes the bottleneck for writes. Ranges suit keys whose new values arrive spread out, not in order.

options.text: Send each record to building hash(record number) mod the number of buildings: an even spread, and no directory to keep updated.
options.part2: Over the winter every record went to building hash(record number) mod 4. That alone moved 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records, and with no directory to switch one piece at a time, each of them answered not found from the morning the rule changed until its van came. After that each building filed 300 a night, and nobody waited. In March the Tannery opened and the rule became mod 5: 960,000 records changed building, in 32 vans, and on the first morning all 960,000 were in no building anyone would look in. A question for 1931 goes to all five buildings.
options.senior: A hash spreads new records evenly, and mod N needs no directory. But the number of buildings is inside the formula, so changing it reshuffles almost everything: going from 3 to 4 a record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for both, one in four. The EVCache case in Season 2 met the same trap with cache keys. Keep a fixed number of partitions, far more than buildings, and a directory of which building holds each, so a new building takes only whole partitions.

options.text: Move every record into one much bigger building with two night clerks: one place to look, and no boundary ever to move again.
options.verdict: Trade-off: works now, the ceiling returns
options.part2: In January the county leased the Wool Store, an old warehouse with shelves for 2,000,000 records, and hired a second night clerk. Forty vans moved all 1,200,000 records, and this time Mr Lowther switched the directory as each van landed, so nothing went missing. Two clerks file 1,200 a night and nobody waits. A question for 1931 goes to one building. It works. But at 1,200 a night the county files 438,000 records a year, so the last 800,000 shelves fill in under two years. And on the night of the Ellingham deposit in April, 3,600 records came in and 2,400 waited at dawn.
options.senior: One bigger machine, scaling up, is the honest first answer: no shard key, no partitions, every question in one place, and nothing that crosses buildings. It buys time, not room. One building's shelves and one door are still the limits, and growth reaches them again. Copies wouldn't help either: read replicas, from s2e12 and s3e05, hold every record and take every write, so they spread lookups, never writes or storage. Shard when growth will pass the biggest building you can get.

sim.title: Split the Kelderby archive
sim.lede: You're Mr Lowther at noon on Monday 2 November, with 1,200,000 records in three buildings, numbered in the order they were filed. Pick how records are split: by year, where a new building takes the newer half of the newest building's records (as now) or only the next year's; by a hash of the record number mod the number of buildings; by a hash of the record number into fixed partitions (12, 120 or 1,200), with the directory saying which building holds each partition; or into one bigger building with two night clerks. Open a building to add one: the sim works out which records must move, and vans carry 30,000 a day, landing at 17:00. Choose whether the directory switches at once (as now) or entry by entry as each piece lands. Each night 1,200 new records arrive, all dated this year, and a night clerk files 600; the vans carry only the records on the shelves at noon on Monday. Turn on the Ellingham deposit for 2,400 papers from 1931 under one deposit number, then key it by deposit and item number. Ask for every record from 1931, or look up No. 1,200,000. The sim's hash multiplies the record number by 7,919 and keeps the remainder after dividing by 1,200,000, which spreads consecutive numbers perfectly evenly; a real hash is only nearly even. Changing the split, the partitions or the directory replays from Monday noon. Click any box to see what it holds.
sim.tryThis: Try this: open a building and look up No. 1,200,000. It's in no building, and 120,000 records can't be found. Send vans until Thursday's lands, and look again. Switch the directory to entry by entry, which replays, and open again: nothing goes missing, but the Ropewalk still takes all 1,200 a night. Try hash mod buildings: 400 each, but opening a fourth moves 900,000 records. Then 120 fixed partitions: 300,000, a quarter. Ask for 1931 under each. Turn on the Ellingham deposit, then key it by item. Last, try 12 partitions and open a fifth building.

explain.oneLine: No record was lost. At noon on Monday the directory was switched for 120,000 records whose boxes were still on the Glasshouse's shelves, so each one sat in no building anyone would look in until its van landed. And splitting by year meant every new record still went to one building: now the Ropewalk.

steps.title: One building runs out of shelves and hands.
steps.text: A database on one machine has two limits that copies can't lift: how much it can store, and how many writes it can take. Read replicas, from s2e12 and s3e05, copy every record, so they share the lookups, but each copy still holds every record and applies every write. Sharding, or partitioning, splits the records instead: each building, or machine, holds a part and takes the writes for that part. The shard key is the value that decides which part a record goes to, and it decides everything after: where new records land, which questions one building can answer alone, and what moves when a building opens. Kelderby's shard key is the year.

steps.title: Ranges keep neighbours together, and dates run hot.
steps.text: Range partitioning gives each building a run of key values: 1850 to 1939, 1940 to 1999, 2000 onward. Records with nearby keys sit together, so a range query, every record from 1931, is one range scan in one building. But a key that only grows, like a date or a number given in order, sends every new record to the building with the newest range. That's a hot partition: the Glasshouse got 1,200 a night while the average building got 400, and 600 waited at dawn. Opening the Ropewalk for 2013 onward didn't cure it. It moved it: 1,200 at the Ropewalk against an average of 300. MongoDB's docs say the same of an always-increasing shard key: every insert goes to one chunk, and its shard becomes the bottleneck for writes.

steps.title: Hashes spread the writes, and range questions go everywhere.
steps.text: Hash partitioning puts a record where a hash of its key says. Neighbouring record numbers land in different places, so new records spread evenly: 400 a building with three, 300 with four. The price is the range query. A record's number says nothing about its year, so every record from 1931 means asking every building and merging the answers, called scatter and gather, and the answer comes only when the slowest building replies. A by-date index inside each partition makes each building's share quick, but not the trips. And a hash can't spread one key that carries too much. The Ellingham deposit, 2,400 papers under one deposit number, lands on one partition: 2,700 tonight at the Ropewalk against an average of 900. Salt the key, deposit number plus item number, and the papers spread, 900 a building, at the cost of asking every partition to gather the deposit back.

steps.title: Rebalancing: move whole partitions, and keep the directory honest.
steps.text: The simplest hash rule, building = hash mod the number of buildings, has the count inside the formula. Change it and almost everything moves, as the EVCache case warned for cache keys: from 3 to 4 buildings a record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder for both, one in four, so 900,000 of 1,200,000 records move. Instead, hash into a fixed number of partitions, many more than buildings, say 120, and keep a directory, also called a partition map, of which building holds each. A fourth building takes 30 whole partitions, a quarter of the records, 300,000, and no even split can move fewer. Then route every lookup through the directory, and change a partition's entry only once it has landed: copy, switch the entry, then clear the old shelves. Kelderby switched the directory for 120,000 records at noon on Monday, while their boxes were still on the Glasshouse's shelves.

steps.title: Shard-aware IDs, and what sharding costs.
steps.text: Instagram's 2012 IDs put the shard in the ID. Like the Snowflake-style numbers of s2e14 they are 64-bit integers that start with 41 bits of milliseconds. Where Snowflake keeps a 10-bit machine number and a 12-bit count, Instagram keeps 13 bits of logical shard ID, up to 8,192 shards, and 10 bits of sequence, 1,024 IDs per shard per millisecond. Its several thousand logical shards map to far fewer database servers, and moving a set of them to a new server changes no ID. Anything holding an ID knows its shard without asking. The cost of all sharding is work that crosses shards. A query without the shard key goes everywhere, and a transaction that changes records in two buildings can no longer be one local transaction of the kind s3e02 covered: it needs a protocol such as two-phase commit, or a shard key chosen so records that change together live together.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for four buildings. The night intake, 1,200 new records a night, 300 to each building. The directory lists 120 fixed partitions and switches entry by entry as each partition lands. The Maltings, the Drill Hall, the Glasshouse and the Ropewalk each hold 30 partitions and take 300 new records a night. Opening a fifth building moves 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, with none unreachable.

notes.text: Opening a fifth: 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, none unreachable

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for four buildings. A record's partition is a hash of its number, and the directory says which building holds each of the 120 partitions: 30 each, so each building takes 300 of the night's 1,200. When a fifth building opens it takes 24 whole partitions, 240,000 records, and each partition's line in the directory changes only once its copy has landed.

fix.title: The fix: hash into 120 fixed partitions, move whole ones, switch the directory one entry at a time
fix.text: Make the shard key a hash of the record number, into 120 fixed partitions, and give each building 30. New records then spread evenly, 300 a building a night, and nobody waits at dawn. Keep an index by date inside each partition, so a question for a year is quick in each building, though it now goes to every building. Keep the directory as the one list of which building holds each partition, and send every lookup and every new record through it. When a building opens, move whole partitions to it, a quarter of the records for a fourth building and a fifth of them for a fifth, and for each partition copy first, switch its directory line once the copy has landed, and clear the old shelves last. Key anything that arrives in bulk under one number, like a family deposit, by its number and an item number, so it spreads too.

limits: Changing the shard key is itself one big move. Going from years to 120 hashed partitions re-decides every record's building, and with four buildings 900,000 of the 1,200,000 records move once, the same three quarters a hash mod 4 would move. Plan it as a migration, a partition at a time, not a weekend.

The number of partitions is a ceiling and a floor. 120 partitions can never spread over more than 120 buildings, and whole partitions divide unevenly when the count doesn't fit: 12 partitions over five buildings give 300 a night to two of them against an average of 240. Too many cost bookkeeping instead: PostgreSQL's docs warn that too many partitions mean longer query planning and more memory.

Hashing spreads keys, not one key. A deposit under one number, or one customer who writes far more than the rest, still lands on one partition, and salting it means every read of that key asks every piece. Questions that cross partitions, every record from 1931 or a change to two records in two buildings, get slower and harder: scatter and gather for the first, a cross-shard transaction for the second.

explain.seniorTake: Shard when one machine can't hold the data or take the writes, and not before, because every split makes some questions harder. Then pick the shard key from how the data arrives and how it's asked for. Ranges keep neighbours together and answer a range in one place, but a key that only grows makes the newest range hot forever. A hash spreads the writes and sends every range question everywhere. Whatever you hash, hash into many more fixed partitions than machines, keep a map of which machine holds each, and grow by moving whole partitions, copying first and switching each map entry only once its copy has landed, so nothing is ever unreachable. Watch the busiest partition against the mean, because one hot key beats any hash, and design so that records changed together share a shard.

realWorld.title: Instagram, 2012: thousands of logical shards, and the shard in the ID
realWorld.text: Instagram's engineering blog described how it sharded its PostgreSQL data: "Our sharded system consists of several thousand ‘logical’ shards that are mapped in code to far fewer physical shards. Using this approach, we can start with just a few database servers, and eventually move to many more, simply by moving a set of logical shards from one database to another, without having to re-bucket any of our data." Each logical shard is a PostgreSQL schema, and each sharded table exists inside each schema. Its IDs had to be sortable by time, ideally 64 bits, and add as few moving parts as possible, so it turned down a separate Snowflake service and made IDs inside PostgreSQL. Each ID consists of "41 bits for time in milliseconds (gives us 41 years of IDs with a custom epoch)", "13 bits that represent the logical shard ID" and "10 bits that represent an auto-incrementing sequence, modulus 1024. This means we can generate 1024 IDs, per shard, per millisecond". Its worked example: "Let’s say we’re sharding by user ID, and there are 2000 logical shards; if our user ID is 31341, then the shard ID is 31341 % 2000 -> 1341." The post calls the result "Primary keys that are unique across our application (and as a bonus, contain the shard ID in them for easier mapping)." One number to check: 2^41 milliseconds is about 69.7 years, as s2e14 worked out, so the post's 41 years undersells its own layout.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL: range, list and hash, inside one server
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's documentation says "Partitioning refers to splitting what is logically one large table into smaller physical pieces." It offers three built-in forms. Range: "The table is partitioned into “ranges” defined by a key column or set of columns, with no overlap between the ranges of values assigned to different partitions. For example, one might partition by date ranges". List: "The table is partitioned by explicitly listing which key value(s) appear in each partition." Hash: "The table is partitioned by specifying a modulus and a remainder for each partition." On when it pays: "a rule of thumb is that the size of the table should exceed the physical memory of the database server." On how many: "Too many partitions can mean longer query planning times and higher memory consumption", and if you choose one partition per customer while customers are few and large, "it may be better to choose to partition by HASH and choose a reasonable number of partitions". These partitions live in one server; sharding spreads the same idea over several.

realWorld.title: MongoDB: ranged sharding keeps neighbours together
realWorld.text: MongoDB's docs on ranged sharding: "Range-based sharding involves dividing data into contiguous ranges determined by the shard key values. In this model, documents with "close" shard key values are likely to be in the same chunk or shard. This allows for efficient queries where reads target documents within a contiguous range." They add that it works best with a shard key of large cardinality, low frequency, and values that don't change monotonically.

realWorld.title: MongoDB: hashed sharding spreads them out
realWorld.text: MongoDB's docs on hashed sharding: "Hashed sharding provides a more even data distribution across the sharded cluster at the cost of reducing Targeted Operations vs. Broadcast Operations. Post-hash, documents with "close" shard key values are unlikely to be on the same chunk or shard - the mongos is more likely to perform Broadcast Operations to fulfill a given ranged query." It adds that hashed keys "are ideal for shard keys with fields that change monotonically like ObjectId values or timestamps."

realWorld.title: MongoDB: keys that only grow, keys that repeat, and scatter-gather
realWorld.text: MongoDB's guide to choosing a shard key: "If the shard key value is always increasing, all new inserts are routed to the chunk with maxKey as the upper bound." Then "The shard containing that chunk becomes the bottleneck for write operations." Its advice: "If your data model requires sharding on a key that changes monotonically, consider using Hashed Sharding." On repeated values: "If the majority of documents contain only a subset of the possible shard key values, then the chunks storing the documents with those values can become a bottleneck within the cluster." And on queries: "When the queries do not contain the shard key, the queries are broadcast to all shards for evaluation. These types of queries are called scatter-gather queries. Queries that involve multiple shards for each request are less efficient and do not scale linearly when more shards are added to the cluster."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: each partition has a ceiling
realWorld.text: AWS's DynamoDB guide says "Every partition in a DynamoDB table is designed to deliver a maximum capacity of 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second." So the table's total throughput only helps if the work spreads, and the guide's first advice is: "You should design your application for uniform activity across all partition keys in the table and its secondary indexes."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: dates make hot partitions
realWorld.text: The guide warns that "A partition key design that doesn't distribute I/O requests effectively can create "hot" partitions that result in throttling", and rates "Item creation date, rounded to the nearest time period (for example, day, hour, or minute)" as a Bad partition key, along with a device ID where one device "is by far more popular than all the others."

realWorld.title: DynamoDB: write sharding, and its cost
realWorld.text: The guide's fix is write sharding: "for a partition key that represents today's date, you might choose a random number between 1 and 200 and concatenate it as a suffix to the date." The cost: "to read all the items for a given day, you would have to query the items for all the suffixes and then merge the results." A suffix calculated from the order ID instead lets you find one item directly, and either way "you avoid having a single "hot" partition key value taking all of the workload."

asked: How would you shard this table?
Range or hash partitioning: which would you use, and when?
How do you add a shard without downtime?
What's a hot partition, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: First ask whether to shard at all: replicas spread reads, a bigger machine buys time, and sharding is for when one machine can't hold the data or take the writes. Then choose the shard key from the access patterns. It should spread writes, have many distinct values with none far more common than the rest, and put records that are read or changed together on the same shard. Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, so range scans hit one shard, but a key that only grows, like a timestamp or a sequential ID, sends every insert to the newest shard. Hash partitioning spreads writes evenly, but range queries become scatter and gather across every shard, so keep a local index, such as by date, in each partition. Never use hash mod the number of servers: from 3 to 4 servers it moves about three quarters of the keys. Hash into a fixed number of partitions, far more than servers, keep a partition map of which server holds each, and add a server by moving whole partitions: copy a partition, catch up the writes made meanwhile, switch its map entry, then delete the old copy, so no key is ever unreachable and nothing needs downtime. Consistent hashing, the next case, is the other common answer. A hot partition is one shard taking far more traffic than the rest, from a growing key or from one hot key; fix the first by hashing, and the second by salting the key with a suffix, or giving that key its own partition, and watch the busiest partition against the mean. Mention shard-aware IDs, like Instagram's 13-bit logical shard ID, and the cost: cross-shard queries and transactions.

terms.def: A local government archive that keeps a county's registrations: births, marriages, deaths and deeds. Kelderby's is split across buildings.
Recording a birth, marriage, death or deed with the county. Each one becomes a record in the archive.
The number every Kelderby record gets, in the order it was filed, from 1 to 1,200,000. The Monday birth is No. 1,200,000.
The person who files the night's new records in one building. Each Kelderby night clerk files 600 a night.
The new records that reach Kelderby's buildings each night to be filed: 1,200, all dated this year.
The card at Kelderby's front desk that says which building holds which records. Every lookup goes through it. A partition map is the same idea.
Asking for one record by its number: the front desk reads the directory and asks the building it names.
How Kelderby moves records between buildings: 30,000 records a day, landing at 17:00.
A collection of papers handed to an archive in one go, often by a family or a firm, and filed under one deposit number.
2,400 papers from 1931 that the Ellingham family's solicitors bring in one night, all under one deposit number.
The value that decides which partition, and so which machine, a record lives in. Also called the partition key. Kelderby's is the year.
Giving each partition a run of key values, such as 1850 to 1939. Records with neighbouring keys sit together.
Putting each record where a hash of its key says. Neighbouring keys land in different partitions, so records spread evenly.
Placing a record on machine number hash(key) mod N, where N is the number of machines. When N changes, most records move.
A question for every record between two key values, such as every record from 1931.
Reading a run of neighbouring keys in order, from one place. Under range partitioning a range query is one range scan in one partition.
A key that only grows, such as a date, a timestamp or a number given in order. Under ranges every new record lands in the last partition.
MongoDB's phrase for a sequential key: one whose values only increase, or only decrease.
Some key values carrying far more records or traffic than others, so their partition runs hot even when keys are hashed.
Adding a suffix, such as an item number, to a busy key so its records spread over several partitions. Reading them back means asking every piece.
A set number of partitions, many more than machines, chosen once. Machines hold whole partitions, and a new machine takes some of them whole.
A logical shard is one of many fixed partitions; a physical shard is the server that holds several of them. Instagram maps thousands of logical shards to far fewer servers.
Instagram's word for deciding again which shard every row belongs to, as changing hash mod N does. Moving whole logical shards avoids it.
A table of which machine holds each partition, read to route every request. Kelderby's directory is one.
Sending each request to the machine that holds its record, by a rule such as hash mod N or by reading a partition map.
Moving partitions or records between machines so each holds a fair share, as when a machine is added or removed.
The order for moving a partition with nothing unreachable: copy it to its new home, switch its map entry, then clear the old copy.
A record the directory sends to a building that doesn't have it yet. The sim counts these as records nobody can find right now.
The sim's hash: 7,919 times the record number, keeping the remainder after dividing by 1,200,000. It spreads consecutive numbers perfectly evenly; a real hash is only nearly even.
The sim's measure of a hot partition: the most new records any building gets tonight against the mean. An even spread makes them equal.
Sending one query to every partition and merging the answers. It is as slow as the slowest partition. MongoDB calls these scatter-gather queries.
MongoDB's names for queries sent to every shard and queries sent only to the shard that holds the key.
An index on the date inside each partition, so it can find its records from one year without reading them all.
A query that needs records from more than one shard, so it must ask several and merge the answers.
A transaction that changes records on more than one shard. It can't be one local transaction, so it needs a protocol such as two-phase commit.
A protocol where a coordinator asks every machine to prepare a change and tells them all to commit only if all said yes. Slower, and stuck if the coordinator fails mid-way.
An ID that carries its shard's number, so anything holding it can tell where the record lives. Instagram's IDs hold 13 bits of logical shard ID.
The last 10 bits of an Instagram ID: an auto-incrementing number, modulus 1024, so one shard can make 1,024 IDs a millisecond.
A photo-sharing app. Its engineers described sharding PostgreSQL and making shard-aware IDs in 2012.
A named group of tables inside one PostgreSQL database. Each Instagram logical shard is one, so one server can hold many.
Splitting one table into partitions inside one PostgreSQL server, by range, list or hash. It doesn't spread the table across servers.
A document database that can spread a collection over many shards, by ranges or by hashes of a shard key.
A range of shard key values and the documents in it. MongoDB moves chunks between shards to balance them.
MongoDB's marker for a value above every other shard key value. The last chunk's range runs up to it, so an always-growing key keeps landing there.
MongoDB's measures of a shard key: how many different values it has, and how often each one occurs. Few values, or a few very common ones, make chunks that can't spread.
MongoDB's query router. It sends a query that has the shard key to the shard holding it, and one without the key to every shard.
MongoDB's default document ID, 12 bytes, which starts with a timestamp, so new ones only grow.
An extra index on a DynamoDB table so items can be found by an attribute other than the table's own key.
Input and output: the reads and writes a database makes to its storage.
One app serving many customers, called tenants, from shared machines and databases.
Software as a service: an app a company rents to its customers over the web instead of selling them a copy.
The ISO/IEC 27001:2022 control that expects the use of resources to be monitored, and future capacity needs projected, so systems keep enough room.

atWork: Picture a multi-tenant SaaS product that put each customer's rows on one of eight PostgreSQL databases by a hash of the customer id. It ran evenly for two years. Then its biggest customer ran a year-end import, one database sat at 95% CPU while seven idled, and every smaller customer sharing that database waited. The fix the team wanted, a ninth database by hash mod 9, would have moved almost every row. Look for both in your own systems. For each sharded or partitioned store, from PostgreSQL partitions to DynamoDB tables to a MongoDB cluster, write down the shard key, then measure the busiest partition against the mean, not just the total: DynamoDB's CloudWatch Contributor Insights, from s2e11, shows the most-used partition keys, and in PostgreSQL a count of rows per partition shows the skew. Ask whether the key only grows, as dates and order numbers do, and whether one tenant can outgrow a partition. Then read how a shard is added: is it hash mod N, or whole partitions moved under a map, and does the map switch before or after the data lands? If you are heading for Build Night L4, the Loadout data tier, rehearse this before you build: model key skew on purpose, give one key forty times the writes of the rest, watch its partition run hot, then salt it and watch the busiest partition fall back towards the mean. If your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.6 (capacity management) expects the use of resources to be monitored and future capacity needs projected; per-partition load against the mean, and a written plan for adding a shard before the busiest one fills, are the kind of evidence an auditor asks for, so build them in now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: A multi-tenant app keeps its orders in four PostgreSQL databases, choosing each order's database by hash(customer id) mod 4. A retailer runs a flash sale, and its database sits at 95% CPU while the other three idle. Next month the team wants a fifth database. What's going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: One customer's key carries most of the writes: a hot partition from key skew, and no hash can spread a single key
Split or salt that customer's key across several partitions, or give it a partition of its own
Going from mod 4 to mod 5 moves about four fifths of the rows; hash into many fixed partitions with a map instead, and move whole partitions

recall.model: The retailer is a hot key. Every one of its orders has the same customer id, so the same hash and the same database: a hot partition from key skew, and no hash can spread a single key. Split that customer's key, for example customer id plus a suffix from 1 to 8 taken from the order number, so its orders spread over several partitions, at the cost of asking all of them to list its orders; or give a customer that big its own shard. And don't go to mod 5: changing the count moves about four fifths of the rows, and each is unreachable until it lands. Hash into a fixed number of partitions, far more than databases, keep a partition map of which database holds each, and move whole partitions to the fifth database, copying each one first and switching its map entry once the copy has landed.

recall.prompt: Records go to building hash(record number) mod the number of buildings, and the hash spreads them evenly. A fourth building joins three. Roughly what share of the records changes building?
options: None: only new records go to the new building
recall.why: A record stays only if its hash leaves the same remainder divided by 3 and by 4, which happens for 3 of every 12 values: a quarter stay and three quarters move. In the sim, 900,000 of 1,200,000. A quarter is what moving whole fixed partitions costs, and it's the least any even split can move.

recall.prompt: Instagram's 2012 post describes 64-bit IDs made inside PostgreSQL. How are the bits split?
options: 41 bits of time, 10 bits of machine number, 12 bits of count
41 bits of time, 13 bits of logical shard ID, 10 bits of sequence
48 bits of time, then the rest random
32 bits of shard ID, then 32 bits of auto-increment
recall.why: The post lists 41 bits for time in milliseconds, 13 bits that represent the logical shard ID, and 10 bits of an auto-incrementing sequence, modulus 1024: 1,024 IDs per shard per millisecond. The first choice is the Snowflake-style layout of s2e14. Instagram put the shard where the machine number was, so any ID says which logical shard holds its row.

recall.prompt: A table of sensor readings is split across 6 shards by ranges of timestamp. What happens to new writes, and to a query for one hour of readings?
options: Writes spread evenly, and the hour's query asks all 6 shards
Writes spread evenly, and the hour's readings sit on one shard
Every new reading lands on the newest shard, and the hour's readings sit on one shard
Every new reading lands on a random shard, and the hour's query asks all 6 shards
recall.why: Timestamps only grow, so with ranges every insert goes to the shard holding the newest range, a hot partition, as at the Glasshouse. In exchange, an hour of readings is one range scan on one shard. Hashing the timestamp would spread the writes and turn the hour's query into scatter and gather.

recall.prompt: You're moving one partition to a new server while the app keeps running. In which order should the steps go?
options: Switch its map entry, copy the partition, then clear the old copy
Switch the whole map at once, then copy the partitions over a few days
Copy the partition, switch its map entry, then clear the old copy
Clear the old copy, then copy the partition and switch its map entry
recall.why: Copy first, so the new home holds everything before anyone is sent there; switch the entry, so lookups go to the copy; clear the old copy last. Switching first, for one partition or all of them, leaves those records unreachable until they land, as Kelderby's directory did for 120,000 records. Real systems also catch up the writes made during the copy just before the switch.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 8 months later. Kelderby runs on 120 fixed partitions now, and in June the Coach House opened as the sixth building. Mr Lowther moved its 20 partitions one at a time: copy, change the partition's line in the directory, clear the old shelves. Lookups never failed. But the night intake desk sorts each night's sacks by its own printed copy of the directory, which it prints on Mondays. On Wednesday night it filed 312 new records at the buildings its printout named, for partitions that had moved to the Coach House on Tuesday. On Thursday the day staff cleared those partitions' old shelves into the basement store, as the plan said, and the 312 went with them. On Friday a man came in for his marriage certificate, registered on Wednesday. No building has it.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened, and what should Mr Lowther change?

keyIdeas.idea: The intake desk routed by an out-of-date copy of the directory, so new records went to a partition's old home after its entry had switched
One directory as the source of truth, read for every new record; a building refuses or forwards records for partitions it no longer holds
Recover the records from the cleared shelves and file them in their partitions; clear an old home only after its last writes are caught up and nothing can be sent there

coldCase.model: The intake desk filed Wednesday's records by its Monday printout, a stale copy of the directory, so 312 records went to the old homes of partitions that had already moved and whose entries had already switched. Every lookup then went to the Coach House, which never got them, and the old shelves were cleared with those records on them. Make one directory the source of truth: the intake desk reads it for every sack, never a weekly copy, and a building refuses, or forwards, any record for a partition it no longer holds, so a stale copy fails loudly instead of quietly. Clear an old home only after its last write has been caught up and nothing can still be sent there. Then go through the cleared boxes, recover the 312 records and file them in their partitions.

sources.title: Instagram Engineering, Sharding & IDs at Instagram (2012; dated 30 December 2012 on its Medium blog), read in the Internet Archive's copy of 12 January 2021, because the live address could not be reached when this case was written (several thousand logical shards mapped in code to far fewer physical shards; moving a set of logical shards without re-bucketing; each logical shard a Postgres schema; 41 bits for time in milliseconds, 13 bits of logical shard ID, 10 bits of auto-incrementing sequence modulus 1024; the 2000 logical shards and user 31341 example)

PostgreSQL 18 documentation, 5.12 Table Partitioning (splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces; range, list and hash partitioning; the rule of thumb that the table should exceed the server's physical memory; too many partitions mean longer query planning and more memory; one partition per customer against HASH with a reasonable number of partitions)
MongoDB Database Manual, Ranged Sharding (contiguous ranges of shard key values; close values likely in the same chunk or shard; efficient queries over a contiguous range)

MongoDB Database Manual, Hashed Sharding (a more even data distribution at the cost of targeted operations; close values unlikely on the same shard; broadcast operations for ranged queries; ideal for keys that change monotonically like ObjectId values or timestamps)

MongoDB Database Manual, Choose a Shard Key (cardinality, frequency, monotonically changing keys; always-increasing keys route all inserts to the maxKey chunk, whose shard becomes the write bottleneck; scatter-gather queries are broadcast to all shards)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Designing partition keys to distribute your workload in DynamoDB (hot partitions result in throttling; item creation date rounded to a time period, and one far more popular device, rated Bad)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly in your DynamoDB table (a random suffix from 1 to 200 on the date; querying every suffix and merging the results; calculated suffixes from the order ID; avoiding a single hot partition key value)

Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, Best practices for designing and using partition keys effectively in DynamoDB (each partition designed to deliver a maximum of 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second; design for uniform activity across partition keys)

UpGuard: ISO 27001 Control 8.6, Capacity Management (a summary of the control, not the standard's own text: monitor the utilization of system resources and project future capacity requirements so adequate resources stay available)
